title: Texas State Employee Faces Losing His Job as DACA Renewal Stalls
excerpt: Juan Rodriguez filed to renew his DACA work permit in April. It is still pending, and the permit that supports his state job expires in December.
body:
• Juan Rodriguez, a Texas state employee and DACA recipient, applied to renew his work permit in April; with the request still pending, he fears losing his state job when the permit expires in December, KVUE reported.
  • Rodriguez has written that renewal times have "skyrocketed from one month to four to six months or longer" — far beyond the window USCIS plans around.
  • USCIS strongly encourages recipients to file renewals 120 to 150 days before expiry and says its goal is to process renewals generally within 120 days; a pending renewal does not extend a permit that expires first.
  • If your DACA expires in the next five months, file inside the USCIS 120-to-150-day window now and keep proof of filing — a lapse means no work authorization until approval.

A Texas state employee who has lived in the United States since he was a toddler could lose his job next month, not because his renewal was denied, but because it has not been decided. Juan Rodriguez applied to renew his Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) work permit in April, according to KVUE. With the request still pending, he fears he could lose his state job when the permit expires in December.

Who is affected

The immediate group at risk is current DACA recipients whose employment authorization documents expire while a renewal is pending. DACA itself has two parts — protection from removal, and work authorization — and only the second keeps a recipient legally on a payroll. When a permit expires before USCIS approves the renewal, the recipient has no work authorization during the gap, however early they filed. First-time applicants are a separate group: under court orders, USCIS accepts initial requests but cannot grant them.

Rodriguez's case shows how wide the gap can open. He put himself through school and earned a bachelor's degree in broadcast communication, and covered everything from breaking news to statewide emergencies such as Hurricane Harvey, he wrote in an Austin American-Statesman op-ed summarized by America's Voice. "But right now, our status is precarious," Rodriguez said. "Threats to DACA are real and mounting."

"Our status is precarious. Threats to DACA are real and mounting."

— Juan Rodriguez, DACA recipient

What changed: the wait, not the rule

No new rule ended Rodriguez's authorization. What changed is processing time. Rodriguez has noted renewal times that have "skyrocketed from one month to four to six months or longer." That sits uneasily beside the timeline USCIS plans around: the agency strongly encourages filing 120 to 150 days before expiry and says it maintains a goal of processing DACA renewal requests generally within 120 days. An April filing for a December expiry was earlier than that guidance — and still may not be decided in time.

Texas adds a second layer of risk. A federal appeals court has held the work-authorization part of DACA unlawful while limiting the effect to Texas, and the case is back before the district court to implement that ruling. Rodriguez has pointed to a Texas court order that could strip work protections from 85,000 Dreamers in the state. Separately, FWD.us has said more than 70,000 DACA recipients in Texas are part of the state's workforce.

What to do next

If you hold DACA, the actionable steps are narrow and time-bound. File your renewal inside the USCIS 120-to-150-day window before the expiry date on your approval notice and work permit. If a renewal has been pending more than 105 days, USCIS allows an online inquiry about its status, and the National Immigration Law Center publishes a step-by-step guide for delayed renewals, including its renewal-date calculator. Tell your employer early: a lapse is an authorization problem, not a performance one, and employers cannot lawfully keep a worker on payroll without authorization.

What happens if a permit lapses

On the sources read for this article, the consequence is specific: without a decision, there is no work authorization during the gap, and a state employee in Rodriguez's position faces losing the job the permit supports. What to watch is whether USCIS decides his renewal before the December expiry — and whether the Texas district court's implementing order changes work authorization for recipients across the state.
